861.quote_or_event: “He alone is known as a spiritual hero, who fights in defense of religion.”
861.explanation: Kabir defines the true hero not by the strength of the foe he chooses but by the cause he fights for.
861.tie_back: The Kural advises avoiding stronger foes and taking on weaker ones; Gurbani measures the warrior instead by the righteousness of his cause, whatever the odds.
861.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1105, Raag Maaroo, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
861._accuracy_note: Next-best and largely a contrast: Sikh ethics judge a fight by its cause, not by picking weaker opponents, and the Sikh tradition honours those who stood against far stronger powers.

862.quote_or_event: In 1699 Guru Gobind Singh instituted the Khalsa, a purified and reconstituted Sikh community bound together as a disciplined order of saint-soldiers committed to courage and to Sikh ideals.
862.explanation: By founding the Khalsa the tenth Guru joined his followers in one loyal brotherhood and gave it the strength to defend itself.
862.tie_back: The Kural says a man without love for his own people, without allies and without strength cannot break an enemy; Guru Gobind Singh's Khalsa built exactly those three things, a devoted people, a brotherhood and armed strength.
862.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, articles Khalsa and Guru Gobind Singh (paraphrase)
862._accuracy_note: Next-best: the Khalsa embodies loyalty, fellowship and strength, but it was founded as a spiritual and moral order, not as the Kural's political calculation for defeating an enemy.

863.quote_or_event: “One who does not frighten anyone, and who is not afraid of anyone else - says Nanak, listen, mind: call him spiritually wise.”
863.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur names fearlessness, joined to never making others afraid, as the mark of the spiritually wise.
863.tie_back: The Kural says the man who is fearful and ignorant is easy prey for enemies; Guru Tegh Bahadur makes the opposite, fearlessness joined to wisdom, the ideal.
863.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1427, Salok Mahalla 9 (salok 16), Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
863._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on fearlessness and wisdom as the opposite of the Kural's fearful, ignorant man; the salok is about spiritual maturity, not about being hard for enemies to beat, and it does not address unsociability or meanness.

864.quote_or_event: “O anger, you are the root of conflict; compassion never rises up in you. You take the corrupt, sinful beings in your power, and make them dance like monkeys.”
864.explanation: In his Salok Sahaskriti Guru Arjan addresses anger directly: it breeds strife and takes control of those it possesses, making them dance like performing monkeys.
864.tie_back: The Kural says the man whose anger never leaves him and who lacks self-restraint is easy for anyone to defeat; Guru Arjan likewise shows the angry man as no longer his own master but led about by his passion.
864.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1358, Salok Sahaskriti (salok 47), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
864._accuracy_note: Strong fit on unchecked anger making a person controllable and weak; Gurbani frames the defeat as spiritual (by krodh, one of the five thieves) rather than military.

865.quote_or_event: “Greed and sin are the king and prime minister; falsehood is the treasurer.”
865.explanation: In the Asa di Vaar Guru Nanak pictures a corrupt age as a court in which greed rules, sin advises and falsehood keeps the treasury.
865.tie_back: The Kural says a ruler who ignores the right path, does what is unfitting, has no shame and no good character is a delight to his enemies; Guru Nanak pictures the same rule by vice in place of right conduct.
865.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 468, Raag Aasaa, Asa di Vaar (salok, Guru Nanak) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
865._accuracy_note: Next-best: both describe rule without right conduct, but Guru Nanak is diagnosing the moral state of his age, and does not speak of enemies profiting from it.

866.quote_or_event: “Unfulfilled sexual desire and unresolved anger waste the body away, as gold is dissolved by borax.”
866.explanation: In the Dakhni Oankar Guru Nanak says lust and anger eat away the person who harbours them, as borax melts gold.
866.tie_back: The Kural says the enmity of a man blinded by anger and swollen with desire is welcome because he destroys himself; Guru Nanak likewise shows kaam and krodh consuming their own host.
866.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 932, Raag Raamkalee, Dakhni Oankar (pauri 18), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
866._accuracy_note: Near match on the same pair of vices (desire and anger) as self-destroying; Gurbani does not draw the Kural's strategic conclusion that such a foe is welcome.

867.quote_or_event: “Farid, there are dozens who say they are friends; I search, but I cannot find even one.”
867.explanation: Farid laments that many claim friendship, but a true friend is hard to find.
867.tie_back: The Kural warns against one who stays close as a friend yet does unworthy things; Farid likewise exposes the gap between those who call themselves friends and real friendship.
867.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1382, Salok Sheikh Farid (salok 87), Bhagat Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
867._accuracy_note: Next-best: shares the theme of false friends, but Farid's line voices spiritual longing for the true Beloved and gives no advice to turn a false associate into an open enemy.

868.quote_or_event: “The Simmal tree is straight as an arrow; it is very tall, and very thick. But those birds which visit it hopefully, depart disappointed. Its fruits are tasteless, its flowers are nauseating, and its leaves are useless.”
868.explanation: Guru Nanak's image of the silk-cotton tree shows something imposing but without any good quality, so that those who come to it go away and do not stay.
868.tie_back: The Kural says a man with no virtues and many faults ends up with no allies; the Simmal tree, tall but fruitless, likewise keeps no one who comes to it.
868.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470, Raag Aasaa, Asa di Vaar (salok before pauri 14), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
868._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on lack of virtue driving others away; Guru Nanak's point (the salok ends by praising sweetness and humility) is moral, and says nothing of enemies gaining from it.

869.quote_or_event: “Farid, in the midst of this beautiful earth, there is a garden of thorns. Those humble beings who are blessed by their spiritual teacher, do not suffer even a scratch.”
869.explanation: In a salok added to Farid's by Guru Arjan, the world is full of thorns, but those blessed by their spiritual teacher pass through unharmed.
869.tie_back: The Kural says those who fight will not lack joy if their enemies are foolish and fearful; Gurbani instead places the safety of the righteous in the Guru's blessing, not in the weakness of their foes.
869.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1382, Salok Sheikh Farid (salok 82, Mahalla 5), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
869._accuracy_note: Next-best only: Sikhism has no teaching that relishes foolish or cowardly enemies; the parallel is limited to coming through a hostile world unharmed.

870.quote_or_event: “That wretched being, whom no one knows - chanting the Naam, the Name of the Lord, he is honored in the four directions.”
870.explanation: Guru Arjan says that even an unknown, lowly person wins honour everywhere through the Name of God.
870.tie_back: The Kural says glory never comes to one who will not take even the easy gain of opposing an unlearned foe; Gurbani locates the source of lasting honour elsewhere, in the Naam.
870.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 386, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
870._accuracy_note: Next-best and a contrast: both speak of how fame is won, but Sikhism does not seek glory in easy victories over the ignorant, and grounds honour in devotion.
